issues.description: The problem statement and UML refer to a fully implemented class named Meal (constructor and getters). However, the template repository does not provide a Meal implementation (Meal.java is empty) and instead contains an Order class with the same structure as the solution's Meal. This name mismatch (Meal vs Order) in the template will confuse students about which class to use/implement and may lead them to implement Meal again or modify Order incorrectly. The solution repository uses Meal, so the template is structurally inconsistent with both the problem description and the reference solution.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the template consistent with the problem statement: either provide a fully implemented Meal.java in the template (matching the problem description), or if Order is intended, update the problem statement and solution to use Order consistently. Preferably remove or rename the template's Order class to Meal (or add Meal implementation and adjust Main) so students clearly see and use the Meal type described in the exercise.

issues.description: The problem statement and solution refer to a 'Meal' class as the core entity for orders, but the template repository provides an 'Order' class (with name and ingredients) and leaves Meal.java empty. This mismatch (Meal vs Order) creates a mapping barrier: students reading the problem expect to work with a Meal type, yet the starter code exposes Order, causing confusion about which class to use or implement.
issues.suggestedFix: Unify the identifier: provide a Meal class in the template matching the problem description (same fields and getters as the solution). Replace or remove the Order class references in the template (and Main) so that all artifacts consistently use 'Meal'. Alternatively, rename Order.java to Meal.java and update internal references to use Meal.
